new_statements.translation: Gómez Rendón: 'In this connection Jijón y Caamaño aptly noted that, besides the prosodic accent on the penultimate syllable that most Esmeraldeño words have, there would be another that he calls "musical accent" (1940-II: 427) ... [tone] would even explain the fact that paroxytone words are often written with an accent mark, when the norm is not to do so, and that this is apparently done with a contrastive sense (Jijón y Caamaño 1940-II: 426).'

new_statements.rule_in_words: All that can be said rests on the accent marks in Pallares' 1877 Spanish-orthography wordlist: most words appear to be stressed on the penult (Jijón y Caamaño via Gómez Rendón), but the diacritics fall often enough and unpredictably enough that Adelaar infers stress was contrastive (lexical); no rule is recoverable and the language is extinct.
new_statements.exceptions: Jijón y Caamaño's 'acento musical' on the past-participle ending written -àà/-áá/-àã (e.g. yatáale 'finished', sakàãle 'drowned'), which Adelaar reports as a special vowel sound and Gómez Rendón reinterprets as tone.
new_statements.domain_note: Philological inference from written accents on isolated words and short phrases in a single 19th-century wordlist; no phonetic observation of speech; word-level only.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the same and only attestation: the vocabulary collected by J. M. Pallares at Esmeraldas in 1877 for Teodoro Wolf and published by Seler (1902); 'Atacame' (Glottolog name) = 'Esmeraldeño' of Adelaar, Jijón y Caamaño and Gómez Rendón (atac1235). No dialect differentiation is possible.

sources.note: p.33 (typological profile of Esmeraldeño from the Pallares-Wolf corpus, following Jijón y Caamaño 1941 II: 425-480 and Adelaar 2004): most Esmeraldeño words carry prosodic accent on the penultimate syllable (after Jijón y Caamaño 1941 II: 427); Pallares' written accents on paroxytone words appear to be used contrastively (J&C II: 426); J&C's additional 'acento musical' on the participle ending -àãle is reinterpreted by Gómez Rendón as tone.
